Neonatal Brown fur seals, or pups, are born after a gestation period that lasts approximately 368 days [tg = approximately 368 days] when measured at the maternal core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that reflects both the embryonic development and a period of delayed implantation typical of otariids. At birth, these altricial neonates weigh around 5,000 grams [Wwb = around 5,000 grams], a mass that provides them with sufficient energy reserves to sustain them during the initial days of suckling, though they remain entirely dependent on maternal milk. The birthing process, or parturition, typically occurs on land during the austral summer, and the newborn pup is immediately capable of vocalizing to establish the critical mother-offspring bond. This neonatal mass is modest relative to the mother's own size but is consistent with the pattern observed in other eared seals, where a trade-off exists between litter size, which is almost always a single pup, and the investment per offspring. The high-fat content of the milk, which can exceed 50 percent lipid, allows for rapid mass gain in these neonatal individuals during the nursing period.

Under the same thermal conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], which represents the standard core temperature of an active, healthy individual, the weaning process for a pup is completed after approximately 354 days since birth [tx = approximately 354 days since birth]. This extended period of nutritional dependence, lasting nearly a full year, is one of the longest among the fur seals and is thought to be correlated with the relatively unpredictable and patchy distribution of prey resources in their Southern Ocean habitat. During this suckling juvenile phase, the pup gradually transitions from an exclusive milk diet to incorporating solid food, a dietary shift that culminates in the cessation of maternal provisioning. The protracted nutritional independence onset allows the pup to develop critical foraging skills under the guidance of its mother, a crucial period for learning hunting techniques. This weaning age contributes to a slow life-history pace, where considerable time is invested in each single offspring before the mother is free to breed again, thereby influencing the maximum reproductive rate of the population.

The sexes in Brown fur seals exhibit one of the most dramatic examples of size dimorphism among pinnipeds, a difference that becomes especially apparent as individuals reach adulthood. The ultimate wet weight for females typically stabilizes around 55,000 grams [Wwi = around 55,000 grams], a body mass that supports their reproductive role and ability to undertake long foraging trips during lactation. In stark contrast, males continue to grow for several more years, ultimately achieving an asymptotic mass of approximately 230,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 230,000 grams] for the largest territorial bulls. This extreme divergence in adult body mass is a direct consequence of intense sexual selection, where larger males have a significant advantage in combat for access to breeding territories and harems of females. The energetic demands of attaining and maintaining such a massive frame, roughly four times that of the female, impose substantial costs, including higher food intake requirements and a greater risk of predation during the extended growth phase. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate wet weight is a defining characteristic of the species.

Puberty, marking the onset of reproductive maturity, arrives at different ages for the two sexes, reflecting the distinct life-history strategies of males and females. For females, the time since birth at puberty is approximately 1,276 days since birth [tp = approximately 1,276 days since birth] when assessed at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], equating to roughly three and a half years of age. In males, the attainment of sexual maturity occurs considerably later, with puberty estimated at approximately 1,643 days since birth [tp = approximately 1,643 days since birth] at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] — a delay that reflects the protracted growth trajectory required to compete for territories. This delayed maturation in males is not a physiological constraint per se but rather a reflection of the social system; young males are rarely able to compete successfully for territories until they have attained a sufficient body size, often several years after physiological puberty has been reached. This phenomenon, known as social or functional maturity, means that although a male may be capable of producing sperm by roughly 1,643 days, his first successful breeding event may be deferred for several more years, a classic example of an age-structured reproductive strategy in polygynous mammals.

When considering the entire lifespan of the Brown fur seal at the standard core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], maximum recorded longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 11,717 days [am = approximately 11,717 days], which is the equivalent of just over 32 years. This substantial lifespan allows for a prolonged reproductive window, especially for females who can produce a single pup annually after reaching maturity. The maximum reproductive rate, however, is limited by the interplay of the lengthy gestation and the year-long weaning period. A female can, at best, produce one pup per parturition [N_R_i = one pup per parturition], with a maximum of one reproductive event per year [F_R_i = one reproductive event per year] — the entire cycle from parturition to weaning consumes nearly twelve months. This minimal fecundity is among the lowest of any marine mammal, constrained by the significant maternal investment required to produce a large, precocial neonate and support it through an extended lactation. This slow reproductive rate, combined with a long lifespan, defines a typical 'K-selected' life-history strategy that is highly sensitive to changes in adult survival.
